name: Warewarewa Arashiyama (和レ和レ和 アラシヤマ)

claims.text: GF guide states the food is 「完全に独立した厨房で調理されており、グルテンフリーの安全性を確認しています」 (cooked in a completely independent kitchen, gluten-free safety confirmed).
Operator claim: 「すべてのメニューがグルテンフリー」— no wheat flour anywhere; udon is 玄米 (brown rice) and fry batter is 米粉 (rice flour), so the fryer handles only GF batter.
GF guide notes 「小麦不使用の調味料を厳選」 (wheat-free condiments carefully selected), indicating tamari-style / wheat-free soy and tsuyu.
Dashi is a traditional bonito (かつお)/kombu stock and egg is used widely; only the kombu-water salad udon is flagged plant-based, so vegan cross-contact with fish stock is likely across most dishes.
GF guide advises: 「グルテンフリー以外のアレルギーがある場合は、事前にお店へ確認してください」 (for allergies other than gluten, confirm with the shop in advance).
Whole menu is gluten-free with a separate/independent kitchen — a rare celiac-safe sit-down option in the Arashiyama tourist core.
Run by an established 32-store café group (パンとエスプレッソと / 株式会社日と々と), suggesting consistent operating standards.

name: めん馬鹿一代 (Menbaka Ichidai (Menbaka Fire Ramen))

claims.text: The shop says it uses dedicated pots and utensils to minimize cross-contamination for gluten-free guests, but it is a shared kitchen that also cooks standard wheat ramen, so it is not a fully dedicated gluten-free environment.
The regular menu is a soy-sauce (shoyu) ramen; standard shoyu tare is typically wheat-based. The gluten-free version is a separate reservation-only preparation rather than the default bowl.
Vegan orders are marked with a colored number card placed at the seat so staff serve the correct plant-based bowl, but the shop does not publish details on separate cooking surfaces for vegan items.

Gluten-free, vegan, vegetarian and no-pork (Muslim-friendly) bowls are offered as a reservation-only special set menu booked in advance via TableCheck; the regular walk-in menu cannot be swapped for these, so dietary guests should reserve ahead and state needs clearly.

Rare among ramen shops, this kitchen intentionally caters to gluten-free, vegan, vegetarian and Muslim-friendly diners, with premium rice-flour noodles for gluten-free guests and a fully plant-based vegan fire ramen offered since 2020.
English website, English-speaking staff and online reservations make it straightforward for foreign diners to arrange and confirm special dietary bowls before visiting.

This is a traditional tofu and kappo counter where soy sauce and dashi are central to the cooking, and fried river-fish dishes (such as karaage) are on the menu, so cross-contact with wheat-containing seasonings and shared frying is likely. Gluten-free is not confirmed; treat as not celiac-safe without verifying directly with the shop in advance.

Soy sauce and dashi are pervasive in this style of cooking, and most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. Assume soy sauce here contains wheat unless the shop confirms otherwise. Documented dishes such as duck teriyaki and vinegared/seasoned preparations rely on soy-based seasonings.

Although tofu is the house specialty, dishes are built on dashi (typically fish-based) and the kitchen prepares live river fish and other seafood, so vegan and vegetarian diners should expect significant cross-contact and confirm preparation directly. Even tofu dishes like yudofu are commonly served with fish-based dashi or soy dipping sauce.

This is a kushiage / kushikatsu specialist: skewers are coated in breadcrumbs and deep-fried, and tonkatsu (breaded pork cutlet) is also served, all from the same fryer. The breading is wheat-based and there is no separate gluten-free fryer, so the oil and prep surfaces carry heavy wheat cross-contamination. Not suitable for celiacs.
Cutlets are hand-breaded with fine breadcrumbs at the counter, confirming wheat coating on the fried items.

As a traditional Japanese izakaya/shokudō, dishes rely on soy-based seasonings and sauces (kushikatsu sauce, dote-yaki, demi-glace), which in Japan almost always contain wheat. Assume soy sauce and sauces here contain wheat unless staff confirm otherwise.

No documented vegan or vegetarian options. The kitchen centers on fried meat skewers, pork cutlet, ham and eggs, and a meat hamburger, and the shared fryer and likely fish/meat-based dashi and sauces mean significant cross-contact even for any vegetable items. Not a reliable choice for vegans.

This is not a celiac-safe restaurant. The menu is built around wheat- and soy-heavy Japanese cooking: dashi broths, soy sauce, vinegared mackerel sushi, and tempura fried in a wheat batter. The official site and listings state no gluten-free menu and no accommodation.
Tempura of seasonal vegetables is a core part of the menu, which means a shared fryer and wheat batter in the kitchen; no dedicated gluten-free fryer is mentioned anywhere.

Soy sauce is used throughout, and most Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat. Dishes such as sashimi, simmered items, and the mackerel sushi rely on soy sauce and dashi, so gluten is present across the menu. No wheat-free tamari is mentioned.

This is a seafood-forward izakaya whose dashi is made from bonito (fish) flakes and kombu, and the kitchen centers on fish, meat, and soy sauce. There is no stated vegan or vegetarian menu, and even vegetable dishes are likely seasoned with fish-based dashi or soy sauce.

This is a market workers' canteen where wheat and soy run through nearly the whole menu: Kitakata soy-based ramen, udon, soba, fried foods, and fish simmered in soy sauce. A shared kitchen and self-serve side-dish counter make cross-contact with wheat effectively unavoidable. It is not suitable for celiacs.

Core dishes are built on soy sauce, including soy-based Kitakata ramen and fish simmered in soy and sugar (sakana no nitsuke). Standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so these dishes should be assumed to contain gluten.

The food is centered on fish, egg, and meat (sashimi, soy-simmered fish, dashimaki tamagoyaki, nikujaga), and broths and seasonings rely on dashi and soy. Even vegetable side dishes are likely seasoned with fish-based dashi. There is no vegan offering, and cross-contact with animal ingredients at the self-serve counter is likely.

Not celiac-safe. The core product is gyoza with wheat-flour skins made from scratch in-house, and the wrappers are pan-fried on the same surfaces used for the rest of the menu, so gluten is unavoidable and cross-contact is effectively certain.
The menu is built around wheat-heavy items (gyoza, ramen, Chinese dishes), so a shared cooking environment with flour and wheat-based noodles should be assumed.
Gyoza are typically served with a vinegar-and-soy-sauce dip and chili oil. Standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so the dipping sauce should be treated as a gluten source.
Not vegan. The gyoza filling contains meat, and the kitchen serves tonkotsu (pork-bone) ramen and other meat-based Chinese dishes, so animal products and shared cooking surfaces are pervasive.

Not celiac-safe. This is a dashi-heavy, soy- and miso-heavy Kyoto obanzai kitchen. Obanzai and miso soup are built on dashi, and dishes lean on soy sauce, miso and pickles, so gluten exposure is broad and cross-contact is hard to control for celiacs.

The menu includes fried items that are wheat-based or batter-based, including 串カツ (kushikatsu, breaded skewers) and 生麩の揚げ出し (agedashi nama-fu, fried wheat gluten). Nama-fu is made from wheat gluten and is not gluten-free, and breaded/fried items share oil and prep surfaces.

No gluten-free or allergen accommodation is published on the restaurant's site or listings. There is no indication of a dedicated fryer or separate prep for gluten-free guests, so a dedicated fryer cannot be assumed.

Soy sauce, miso and Saikyo miso marinades feature heavily (e.g. 銀鱈 西京漬け silver cod in Saikyo miso, 牛頬肉の赤味噌 braised beef cheek in red miso). Most Japanese soy sauce and many miso products contain wheat, so these dishes should be treated as containing gluten unless individually confirmed.

Vegan is very difficult here. Obanzai and miso soup are made with fish-based dashi, the breakfast and many dishes include egg (dashimaki tamago) and grilled fish, and seafood is central to the menu. Even vegetable dishes are likely simmered in dashi.
No vegetarian or vegan options or labeling are published. A diner avoiding all animal products should call ahead to ask whether any vegetable dishes can be prepared without dashi, egg or fish.
No published allergen policy or gluten-free menu. For any dietary needs, call the restaurant directly at 075-231-1354 to discuss before visiting; celiac-level cross-contamination cannot be assured.

The kitchen says it personally sources seasonal ingredients and pays attention to safety and quality, and cooks to order (e.g. clay-pot rice), which can make it easier to have a direct conversation about ingredients when you book ahead.
